topic.title: Neural Learning Dynamics and Constructive Architectures
topic.overview: This historically broad cluster asks how neural networks acquire internal representations, how their architecture should grow, and why training can overfit. Early examples examine perceptrons, hidden-unit construction, alternative learning objectives, and regularization. Later papers revisit model symmetries and local learning mechanisms, with some constructive architectures offering interpretable alternatives to end-to-end backpropagation.
topic.whyItMatters: Representing a function is different from learning it reliably from finite data. Architecture, training dynamics, and stopping rules interact, so even a realizable task can produce poor generalization.
topic.evolution: The collection begins with foundational network classifiers and decision systems in 1987. Work through the 1990s studies internal-representation search, node splitting, weight decay, and overfitting in simple models. Recent representatives explore connectivity between trained solutions, alternative credit assignment, and forward-growing polynomial forecasters; these are related questions, not evidence of one uninterrupted research lineage.
openQuestions: Which constructive architectures retain competitive performance while exposing useful structure?
How can simple learning models reveal failures that persist at modern scale?
